claims.text: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state has a native oxide layer formed during ambient-air exposure.
The native oxide on Q235 steel is a mixture of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
At room temperature, the native oxide is self-limiting and protective.
At 700–900 °C in aggressive molten salts, chloride and sulphide species flux and disrupt the native oxide.
Disruption of the oxide at high temperature causes spallation and accelerated degradation.
Oxide-layer thickness, phase composition, and adhesion mediate the effect of environment on corrosion performance.
At room temperature, slow oxide-scale growth produces adherent layers that limit further corrosion.
In high-temperature molten salts, aggressive species promote oxide disruption through thermal-expansion mismatch.
Capillary action contributes to disruption of the oxide layer in high-temperature molten salts.
Oxide spallation exposes fresh Q235 steel that is susceptible to rapid oxidation.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, cyclic exposure at 700–900 °C in Na2SO4/NaCl will increase the mass of Q235 specimens.
Cyclic high-temperature molten-salt exposure will cause observable oxide spallation and degradation.
Cyclic high-temperature molten-salt exposure will decrease hardness or oxide adhesion relative to the room-temperature baseline.
As-received Q235 steel under benign room-temperature conditions experiences minimal fluxing and retains protective behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies to untreated and uncoated Q235 steel.
A deliberately enhanced adherent oxide layer may prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.
Alloying elements that substantially modify oxidation behavior may prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.

contradictions.description: The causal account invokes chloride and sulphide species, but the specified test salt is Na2SO4/NaCl, which supplies sulfate rather than sulphide. No conversion pathway from sulfate to sulphide is proposed or measured.
